- PREPARED 4-6 EXAM-AUTHENTIC QUESTIONS PER CONCEPT:

    * [Q1] (1-mark MCQ): A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of 30° with the mirror surface. What is the angle of reflection?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: 60°
      -> Socratic Hint: Remember that the angle of incidence is measured with respect to the normal (perpendicular to the surface), not the mirror surface itself!
    * [Q2] (2-mark Definition): State the two laws of reflection of light.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: (1) The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. (2) The incident ray, normal to the mirror at the point of incidence, and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane.
      -> Socratic Hint: Recite both the angular equality and the coplanar requirement.
  * Concept #2 "Plane Mirror Image Properties":
    * [Q1] (1-mark MCQ): If an object is placed 10 cm in front of a plane mirror, what is the distance between the object and its image?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: 20 cm
      -> Socratic Hint: The image is formed as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. Calculate total distance object-to-image.
    * [Q2] (PYQ): Why is the image formed by a plane mirror called a virtual image?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Because the light rays do not actually intersect at the image position; they only appear to diverge from it, and it cannot be caught on a screen.
      -> Socratic Hint: Think about whether light rays physically pass through the image location behind the mirror.

chapter_notes: Light is an electromagnetic radiation that enables us to see. By observing common optical phenomena, we conclude that light travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation), indicated as a ray of light. When light falls on a polished surface like a mirror, reflection occurs obeying the laws of reflection: (i) Angle i = Angle r, and (ii) Incident ray, normal, and reflected ray are coplanar. Plane mirrors produce virtual, erect, laterally inverted images of the same size placed at an equal distance behind the mirror. Curved surfaces (like a shining spoon in Activity 9.1) distort or scale images differently, paving the way for spherical mirrors.

chapter_notes: Spherical mirrors have reflecting surfaces that form part of a sphere. A concave mirror curves inwards towards the sphere's centre, while a convex mirror curves outwards. Key terminology includes: Pole (P, centre of reflecting surface), Centre of Curvature (C, centre of the hollow sphere), Radius of Curvature (R, radius of the sphere), Principal Axis (straight line passing through P and C), Principal Focus (F, point where parallel rays converge or appear to diverge), and Focal Length (f, distance between P and F). For small apertures, R = 2f.

chapter_notes: Image formation in spherical mirrors uses ray diagrams governed by four key rules: (i) Parallel rays pass through focus F, (ii) Rays through focus emerge parallel, (iii) Rays through centre of curvature C reflect back along the same path, and (iv) Oblique rays at pole P reflect at equal angles. The New Cartesian Sign Convention sets pole P as origin, object on the left, distances measured right as positive, left as negative, heights above principal axis positive, and below negative. The mirror formula is 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. Magnification m = h'/h = -v/u.

chapter_notes: Refraction is the change in direction of light when it travels obliquely from one transparent medium to another, caused by a change in the speed of light. Laws of refraction: (i) Incident ray, refracted ray, and normal are coplanar, and (ii) Snell's law: sin i / sin r = constant (n21). Absolute refractive index nm = c / v. Optically denser medium has a higher refractive index where light slows down and bends towards the normal. Kerosene has higher optical density than water despite lower mass density.

2. Focal length:

   $f = -\frac{15}{2} = -7.5\text{ cm}$.

worked_examples.problem: End-of-Chapter Exercise Q10 (p. 26): An object 5 cm in length is held 25 cm away from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Draw the ray diagram and find the position, size, and the nature of the image formed.
worked_examples.given: Object height $h_1 = +5\text{ cm}$; Object distance $u = -25\text{ cm}$; Focal length of convex lens $f = +10\text{ cm}$.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Image distance: $v = +\frac{50}{3} \approx +16.67\text{ cm}$ (formed on opposite side of lens, real).
2. Image height: $h_2 = h_1 \times \frac{v}{u} = 5 \times \frac{50/3}{-25} = 5 \times \left(-\frac{2}{3}\right) = -\frac{10}{3} \approx -3.33\text{ cm}$.
3. Nature: Real, inverted, and diminished (height 3.33 cm).
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Image is real, inverted, located at +16.67 cm behind the lens with height -3.33 cm.
